A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HDR-4DGS work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original HDR/LDR reconstruction experiments on synthetic and real scenes, quantitative comparisons in Tables 1–2, and ablations and visual results in the main text and appendix.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds two-stage reconstruction comparisons, learned tone-mapping curves, and structural-detail comparisons.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.4 retain the same 4D Gaussian representation, radiance bank, dynamic context learner, per-channel tone mapping, and reconstruction losses. Diagram and notation refinements do not establish an algorithmic change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same eight HDR-4D-Syn scenes and four HDR-4D-Real scenes, with unchanged dataset statistics in Tables 7–8. The added analyses reuse this coverage; single-exposure selection is an additional ablation setting. Other camera-rig datasets are cited but not evaluated.

E2.justification: v3 Table 3 adds a distinct comparator family: 4DGS followed by EIN, IntrinsicHDR, KPNet, or KUNet for independent HDR reconstruction. These evaluated alternatives are absent from v1 and substantially broaden comparison beyond integrated rendering and tone-mapping methods. The original comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: The new two-stage experiment trains 4DGS on single-exposure LDR images at 2.0 seconds before applying HDR reconstruction models. Section 4.2 also introduces post-training extraction and timestamp sampling of tone-mapping curves. Existing benchmark splits, metrics, and stated training settings remain unchanged; additional capture documentation does not establish a changed acquisition protocol.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands diagnostic evidence through learned tone-mapping curves in Section 4.2/Figure 4, the joint-versus-two-stage reconstruction experiment in Table 3, and structural-error comparisons against vanilla 4DGS in Figures 10–11. Existing tone-mapper, pixel-supervision, temporal-window, and DRCL ablations are retained; the DRCL analysis moves to Appendix A.2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests for the experiments. Averaging results over scenes remains the reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the retained ablation values are unchanged. New Table 3 reports HDR PSNR values of 17.75, 11.63, 20.92, and 19.00 for the four two-stage alternatives alongside the retained HDR-4DGS value of 25.88, under different input setups. New curves and visual comparisons add supplementary findings about temporal adaptation and structural detail.

T1.justification: The problem formulation and mathematical content of Equations 1–8 are unchanged apart from notation. The new monotonic tone-mapping curves are empirical observations, not new formal guarantees, derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: HDR DNVS, HDR-4DGS with dynamic tone mapping, two benchmark datasets, and claimed quality and efficiency advantages. The added evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations linking tone-curve changes to scene brightness, attributing structural degradation to the base 4DGS representation, and partly attributing real-scene PSNR discrepancies to noisy HDR ground truth. It also argues for joint reconstruction and explicitly discusses the boundary imposed by identical synchronized cameras. Appendix A.3's existing limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly documents Blender synthesis, tripod-mounted capture, calibration from empty-scene images using COLMAP, and maintenance of camera parameters during dynamic capture. The abstract adds a code repository link instead of a release promise, although Section 7 still states that release is forthcoming. Existing hardware, initialization, and hyperparameters remain.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting EIN, IntrinsicHDR, KPNet, and KUNet comparisons, plus camera-rig precedents such as the Google Immersive and Technicolor datasets. These extend comparison and acquisition positioning locally; the main related-work narrative and novelty positioning remain.

P1.justification: v3 adds a dedicated tone-mapping analysis subsection, expands dataset explanations, and moves the DRCL discussion to the appendix. It also makes localized wording, notation, affiliation-layout, and publication-header edits. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds Table 3 and Figures 4, 10, and 11, refines Figure 1's labels and arrows, and adjusts float placement. The DRCL table moves from main-text Table 5 to appendix Table 9, while v1 Figure 12 becomes main-text Figure 6. Existing visual evidence is largely preserved rather than replaced.

improvement.justification: v3 improves support for the unchanged method through direct visualization of learned temporal tone mapping and adds useful capture and calibration details. The new comparisons broaden evaluation, but their single-exposure inputs versus the retained multi-exposure method do not isolate the benefit of joint optimization, limiting the stronger necessity claim in Section 4.4. Overall, the added evidence and documentation provide a modest quality gain while the main results and existing limitations remain.
